posts.author: JohnFP
posts.content_md:
Michael, I think that is a good find. If you have a spare hologram you don't mind doing some tests on, try to repeat the proceedure but then dry the hologram with a blow dryer "hot and heavy" and see if it goes back to the green in minutes instead of days.

If you believe in the molecule binding theory of Myerhofer for DCG alcohol drying then it seems the alcohol left in the emulsion, being highly hydroscopic, has water molecules bound to it. Then the alcohol evaporates more quickly then the water and the water is left in the emulsion. This water give the red appearance. Once the water is taken out the hologram will go back to green.

Now, is this even worth doing? Does the "cleared" hologram seem cleaner the the original? Less noisy? Is their any increase in brightness?

posts.author: MichaelH
posts.content_md:
> **JohnFP:** Michael, I think that is a good find. If you have a spare hologram you don't mind doing some tests on, try to repeat the proceedure but then dry the hologram with a blow dryer "hot and heavy" and see if it goes back to the green in minutes instead of days.

The ability of alcohol to lock-in moisture was [hashed about here](http://www.holographyforum.org/phpBB2/viewtopic.php?t=2726&highlight=alcohol+crust) and I'm not surprised to find that still happening. I even baked the hologram in an attempt to drive more water out but that had no effect. It seems as though the theoretical "crust" was keeping the moisture in.

> **JohnFP:** If you believe in the molecule binding theory of Myerhofer for DCG alcohol drying

Never heard of it before 

> **JohnFP:** Does the "cleared" hologram seem cleaner the the original? Less noisy? Is their any increase in brightness?

I'm doing another test now. I cut a recently made hologram in half, soaked half in distilled water to hydrate it and am now soaking that piece in isopropyl alcohol. In the five minutes it's taken me to finish writing all this I can see that the film is becoming clearer. I don't expect it to be any cleaner or brighter than the unsoaked half but I'll report back later today.

posts.author: Tom B.
posts.content_md:
I assume you were using PFG-01 film that had been bleached with dichromate? And the post treatment was soaking for 5-10 minutes in 1% ascorbic acid under a halogen lamp followed by a thorough rinse.

I just tried this with a very old (several years) PFG-01 hologram and found that soaking in 99% isopropyl alcohol for 20 minutes had no effect at all on the reddish color. I wonder if there is maybe something going on with your more recently processed holograms that's different - like some residual trace of dichromate in the emulsion that is activated by alcohol to bleach the colloidal silver? Presumably this residue becomes less active over time (oxidizes?) so my old hologram didn't show this effect. Well, that's one guess....

I assume this is Philips' ferric EDTA recipe? I never had good results with this with PFG-01 due to excessive noise but it seems others have done better.

My original intent was to duplicate the alcohol bleaching effect on a piece of film, then run it through the redevelopment process again to see if it turned red again, just to see if the silver was still there in a photosensitive form.

I sort of recall seeing a strange effect like this with alcohol once but never bothered to follow it up. I have uncritically accepted the colloidal silver explanation for the reddish tint but have not thought of a way to test it.

posts.author: MichaelH
posts.content_md:
I just dropped my cleared and dried film back in the 1% ascorbic solution and interestingly it went almost immediately (quite literally, in just 2-3 seconds) 50% of the red that it was before being cleared by the alcohol. It was almost like it had a bit of a memory.

After 20 minutes it was a deeper more even red and just slightly darker than the the un-cleared half of the film.

The re-treated half is just as bright as the half that didn't go through the alcohol and I can't see any indication that the alcohol had a positive or negative impact.

What I'm doing now is I've covered half of each test piece to see if there's any difference in print-out behavior.

posts.author: MichaelH
posts.content_md:
Alright, for the last month and a half I've had those two pieces sitting in my south-facing window with the right half covered.

No difference at all in print-out behavior. Both pieces have darkened slightly by the same amount.

Just to gain further data I've covered up half the darkened portion and I'm going to put the holograms back in the window for another month or so.

It's clear that ipa does *something* to holograms that have been post-treated with ascorbic acid but clearly it doesn't do anything that helps prevent print-out.

It's also clear that ascorbic doesn't prevent print-out although this test won't show by how much it might reduce it.
